Base-enabled access to diastereoselective
spirofuran oxindoles and c-functionalized
allenoates†
Basavaraja D., ab Ajay Krishna M. S., a Jagadeesh Krishnan, a Athira C. S., ab
Amrutha R. R., a Eringathodi Suresh
 c and Sasidhar B. Somappa
 *ab
Base assisted divergent reactivity of isatins and allenoates has been
achieved, which aﬀorded diastereoselective spirofuran oxindoles
and c-functionalized allenoates. The DBU mediated Morita–Baylis–
Hillman (MBH) reaction followed by the cascade annulation through
the stabilized b-ammonium enolate intermediate led to the spiro-
framework, wherein DABCO furnished thec-functionalized allenoates.
The protocol offers access to biologically relevant functionalized
oxindole scaffolds with an excellent substrate scope under mild reaction
conditions.
Oxindole is a vital pharmacophore present in many bioactive
natural products and has attracted greater attention due to its
significant pharmaceutical properties.
1 The functionalized and
spirooxindole hybrids have also displayed various medicinal
properties.
2 A few structures with a spirooxindole core are
highlighted in Fig. 1. Spirotryprostatin A is an inhibitor of
G2/M progression of cell division in mammalian cells. 3 The
first macroline-related oxindole alkaloid Alstonisine is known
to exhibit antimalarial properties,
4a and several spirooxindole
cores presently are being explored for antiviral therapeutic
potential.
4b Natural product inspired thiazolidinone spiro oxi-
ndole is a selective inhibitor of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis
protein tyrosine phosphatase B. 5 On the other hand, a number
of allenic motif containing compounds are also of pharmaceutical
relevance (Fig. 1). For instance , allenic nucleoside analogs,
adenallene, and cytallene are cyt otoxic and antiviral agents,
respectively. Hydroxyl acids and the methyl esters of allenes are
known for their antifungal activity, and Grasshopper ketone is an
allenic naturally occurring carotenoid6 (Fig. 1).
Moreover, the construction of these hybrids is a challenge
for synthetic organic chemists. Subsequently, many research
groups have demonstrated the synthesis of oxindole based
spiro cycles.
7 To highlight a few relevant reports, Jia et al.
reported the synthesis of spirocyclic oxindole-butenolides by
three component [2 +2+1 ] cycloaddition of isocyanides, alleno-
ates, and isatins (Scheme 1). 8 Lu et al. ’s synthesis of chiral
spirooxindoles was reported via an asymmetric [3+2] annula-
tion reaction between allenic esters and isatinimines. 9 Shi and
co-workers have carried out pioneering work in the synthesis of
several privileged spirooxindole motifs.
10 Spiro tetrahydrofuran
oxindoles by the reaction of allenoate phosphine zwitterions
with isatins were developed by Nair’s – group in 2015
(Scheme 1).
11 A three-component reaction by cyclization of
isocyanide, allenoates, and isatins has led to the structurally
complex spirooxindoles.
12 T h el i t e r a t u r er e p o r t se m p h a s i z et h a t
the majority of the spirooxindole chemistry is associated with the
spiro pyrrole/pyrrolidine and spiro pyridine oxindoles.7,9,10 Hence,
spirofuran oxindoles are relativelyless explored for their biological
properties; this signifies the need of novel methodologies for their
synthesis.

In view of these exciting observations and in continuation of
our attention towards the spiro and biologically relevant
heterocycles,
13 it was of great interest to investigate isatin
reactivity towards allenoate zwitterions with reasonable expec-
tations of accessing spirofuran oxindoles in the process. At the
outset, the protocol’s feasibility was first investigated by
the reaction of N-methyl isatin 1 and 3-methyl allenoate 2
in the presence of 1,8-Diazabicyclo [5.4.0]undec-7-ene (DBU,
1.0 equiv.) in acetonitrile at room temperature. After 2 h, the
spirofuran oxindole 3a was obtained in 18% yield as a single
diastereomer. Its molecular structure and relative stereo-
chemistry were established by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(NMR), and High-Resolution Mass (HRM) spectroscopy, and
further confirmed via single-crystal X-ray analysis of one of the
derivatives 3ag (Scheme 2).
The reaction parameters were screened to improve the yield
and overall process; the results are summarized in Table 1.
Firstly, we tuned the stoichiometric ratio of substrates; 1 equiv.
of N-methyl isatin 1 and 0.6 equiv. of 3-methyl allenoate 2
resulted in a 43% yield of 3a. An excess of allenoate (Table 1,
entry 1–4) suppressed the yield. Increment in the DBU loading
to 2 equiv. afforded 56% yield (Table 1, entry 8). Furthermore,
an increase or decrease in DBU loading from 2 equiv. and
catalytic amounts (Table S2, ESI †) did not show any positive
results. Subsequent screening of bases like DMAP, Et
3N, and
DABCO demonstrated that DBU is the best choice (Table 1,
entry 8). Careful screening of the solvents and neat reaction
(Table 1, entries 15–21) indicated that acetonitrile is the most
suitable solvent. Further assessment on variation in the reac-
tion temperature (Table 1, entries 22 and 23) lowered the yields.
Gratifyingly, the time-dependent quenching of the reaction
between 0.5 h and 2 h markedly resulted in an improved yield
of 75% (Table 1, entry 25). By extending the reaction time, the
yield decreased to some extent (Table S2, ESI, † entry 5); this is
due to the formation of complex products (observed in TLC).
Based on these experimental results, the best reaction condi-
tion was confirmed to be 1 equiv. of N-methyl isatin, 0.6 equiv.
of allenoate and 2 equiv. of DBU in acetonitrile at room
temperature for 1 h (Table 1, entry 25).
With the optimized conditions in hand, the reaction’s
versatility has been successfully explored for diversely substituted
isatins with various allenoates (Scheme 2). In all the experiments,
the reaction proceeded smooth ly and furnished the expected
products in moderate to good yiel d s .H o w e v e r ,t h eh i g h e s ty i e l d
of 88% was noticed for compound 3af.S l i g h t l yl o w e ry i e l d sw e r e
o b s e r v e di nt h ec a s eo fN-protected isatins with a bulkier benzyl
group and also for N-protected 5-Bromo isatins. Moreover, it was
found that allenoates having sma ller ester substituents such as
Me and Et, attributed comparatively higher yield than the bulkier
tBu group. Comparably moderate to good yields were obtained
for variously g-substituted allenoates. 5-OMe/5-NO2 isatins and
g-Phenyl allenoates did not furnish the expected cyclized product.
These results highlight the broa d substrate scope of DBU-base
mediated MBH type reaction fo llowed by cascade annulation of
isatins and allenoates.

During the optimization of spirofuran oxindole synthesis,
a serendipitous observation led to the identification of
g-functionalized allenoate 4a (Scheme 3), and it was found that
the reaction between N-methyl isatin 1 and allenoate 2 in the
presence of (1,4-diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane (DABCO)) in acetonitrile
could not furnish the spirofur an oxindoles. Nevertheless, a
diﬀerent product with a slight change in retention factor ( R
f)
value (observed in TLC) was separated and characterized as
g-functionalized allenoate (4a). The structure was unambiguously
confirmed through the single-crystal X-ray analysis of one of the
analogs 4h (Scheme 3). Allenes and thei r functionalized hybrids
were found to be explored for various therapeutic applications. 6
Very recently, Yao et al. reported an NHC-catalyzed regiospecific
g-functionalized alle noate (Scheme 1). 14 Encouraged by the
above results, a systematic optimization has been carried out by
considering the stoichiometric ratio of substrates, catalyst loading,
solvent suitability,etc., to improve the yields (ESI,† Table S1). After
careful observation, 1 equiv. of N-methyl isatin 1, 1.5 equiv. of
allenoate2 and 1.8 equiv. of DABCO in DMSO at 0–5 1Cf o r0 . 5h
(ESI,† Table S1, entry 21) is considered as the best-optimized
condition. Furthermore, we explored the scope of the reaction for
variousg-functionalized allenoates under the optimized conditions.
Including bulky groups such as propyl and benzyl groups on the
nitrogen atom of isatin could furnish the expected product in
59–87% yields, and propargylated isatin gave the product 4s in
54% yield (Scheme 3).
To gain preliminary insight into the reaction mechanism
and resolve how two diﬀerent bases resulted in a diﬀerent
reactivity, we performed a few control experiments (Scheme 4
and Table S2, entries 6, 10, ESI †). In a DBU mediated reaction,
within a minute, we have observed the formation of product 4a
(Scheme 4a); and this was followed by cascade cyclization
between quickly formed 4a and one more molecule of isatin
1a in the presence of the stoichiometric amount of DBU leads
to the formation of 3a. To achieve faster rate, a higher concen-
tration of enolate is required. Here, the DBU will shift the

equilibrium towards the b-ammonium enolate (Scheme 5) by
stabilizing it through conjugation, which increases its equili-
brium concentration; eventually, the reaction rate is enhanced
for further cyclisation.
15 The DBU mediated reaction between
isolated 4a and 1a further confirms the involvement of 4a in
the formation of 3a (Scheme 4b). As shown in Scheme 4c,
the lack of conjugation in DABCO, substantial reduction in
nucleophilicity by incorporating bulky substituents a to nitro-
gen results in steric hindrance to the b-ammonium enolate. 15
This causes a shift in the equilibrium back to 4a. Therefore it
could not initiate further cyclization even after 24 h (Table S2,
entry 10, ESI †).
Based on the experimental results and considering the
previous reports,
11,14,15 we have proposed a plausible mecha-
nism for spirofuran oxindole formation. Initially, the nucleo-
philic addition of DBU to 3-alkyl allenoate 2 occurs, aﬀording a
zwitterion intermediate A. The zwitterion A thus formed can
easily add to the carbonyl carbon of the N-protected isatin 1
to form the intermediate B. After that, the proton transfer
delivers C; the elimination of DBU results in an intermediate
product 4a, which eventually forms stabilized b-ammonium
enolate intermediate D in the presence of a stoichiometric
amount of base. The latter undergoes nucleophilic addition
to the second molecule of isatin furnishing E, which upon
cyclization, leads toF. This intermediate, after proton transfer and
elimination of DBU, delivers the desired product 3a (Scheme 5).
Similarly, the plausible mechanism for g-functionalized
allenoate ( 4) is presented in Scheme S2 (ESI †).
In summary, base mediated divergent reactivity of isatins
and allenoates has been accomplished. These protocols oﬀer a
facile synthetic route to access the spiro and functionalized
oxindoles. In particular, DBU promoted MBH type reaction
provides unprecedented access to the spiro-furan oxindoles of
medicinal importance. The method proceeds under mild reac-
tion conditions and complements a diverse substrate scope.
